tagline: An eel-shaped shark with a collar of frills
summary: A slender, eel-like shark with six frilly gill slits—the first pair meeting across the throat like a ruff—and a mouth lined with rows of small, three-pointed teeth. A primitive-looking deep-water hunter, it swallows squid, fishes and even other sharks, and may carry its young for more than a year.
ability: needle-trap jaws and an extremely long pregnancy

stats.depth: Typically 500–1,000 m; recorded from about 20 to 1,500 m
stats.range: Patchy in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, on outer shelves, slopes and seamounts
stats.diet: Deep-water squid, bony fishes and other sharks

facts.title: Where the name comes from
facts.text: It has six gill slits with frilly edges, and the lower ends of the first pair join across the throat, forming a ruff-like collar.

facts.title: Teeth that point inward
facts.text: Its large mouth holds groups of small, sharp, three-pointed teeth that point inward. It can swallow relatively large prey, including other deep-water sharks.

facts.title: A very long pregnancy
facts.text: Young hatch from eggs inside the mother and feed on large yolky eggs; litters of 2–15 pups are born at about 40–60 cm long. Gestation is thought to last more than a year.

facts.title: First filmed in 2004
facts.text: In August 2004, scientists reviewing submersible video off the south-eastern USA spotted a frilled shark gliding over sandy seafloor—thought to be the first time one was seen alive in its natural habitat.

facts.title: A 'living fossil'?
facts.text: Often called a 'living fossil', it shares many physical features with shark ancestors from the age of dinosaurs, and is described as a primitive deep-water shark.

Gallery: NOAA 2004 in-situ video frame (low quality, burnt-in data overlay; depth 2,866 ft as shown on the frame). Rejected: 'Frill shark - Australian Museum 2022.png' (credited to ChatGPT—AI-generated), 'Deania hystricosa.jpg' (other species). The 2007 Awashima Marine Park live shark images are not freely licensed. A separate southern African species, C. africana, was split off in 2009, so older 'worldwide' ranges may include it. 'Living fossil' is a popular label; the NatGeo source is a photo caption.
